To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
steam explosion of aspenwood in 1% sulfuric acid at 240°C for 3 min gave 90% of the pentosans in solution, and 90% of glucose in water‐insolubles.
(1) Steam explosion pretreatment of aspin wood chips, at 240°C in saturated steam for 5 min, followed by enzymatic hydrolyses, gave 70% of the theoretical yield of glucose and 80% of total sugars.

steam explosion pretreatment is not necessary for efficient enzymatic hydrolyzation of wood to glucose, that the key to the success of steam explosion pretreatment was the dilute sulfuric acid impregnation, that steam explosion pretreated aspenwood was more accessible for enzymatic hydrolysing than wood treated with dilute sulfuric impregnation alone, and that steam explosion pretreatments were not more effective for the production of butanediolo ethanol than were dilute acid impregnations
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of steam to pretreat lignocellulose for enzymatic hydro lysis.
the development of a process for the economical production of fuel ethanol by fermentation of cellulose.
the use of steam to hydrolyze pentosan in wood, and with the use of enzymes to hydrolyze hexosan.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
steam‐explosion of wood, as presently practiced, is a very effective pretreatment for enzymatic hydro lysis.
steam‐explosion is not a necessary step in the conversion of wood to fermentable sugars.
steam explosion is a useful technique for the pretreatment of wood, but that it can be dispensed with in some instances.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

steam explosion of wood is unnecessary, that dilute acid impregnated wood is more readily hydrolyzable than dry steam‐treated wood, and that small chips give more accessible substrate for hydrolysis than large chips.
steam explosion of wood is a convenient method for preparing a substrate with high enzymatic digestibility, but that the explosion step is not essential.
steam pretreatment, with or without explosion, is a useful method to increase the accessibility of cellulose for enzymatic hydrolysate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
steam pretreatment is a promising method for producing fermentable sugars from lignocellulose.
steam‐explosion of wood at 240°C is not necessary for hydrolysis of cellulose and fermentation of the resulting sugars.

the steam‐explosion process is not essential for the production of ethanol from lignocellulosic biomass, and that the process should not be used for this purpose unless the cost of steam is negligible.
